Zenith Standard Time (ZST) would be a boon for health, sociability, safety, and business. With today's technology it would be trivial to automatically coordinate cross-country communications and travel. 

As article states;

Before U.S. railroads introduced standard time zones in 1883, towns set their clocks to strike noon when the sun reached its zenith overhead. As The New York Times put it that November, if clocks had rung an alarm at local noon from Maine to the Pacific, “there would have been a continuous ringing from the east to the west lasting for 3¼ hours.”

Just think: a cross-country trip could take literally no time!

I have a PhD in Food Science and I'm board-certified in preventive medicine. All of a sudden "ultra-processed" is the bogeyman when the problem is salt, sugar and saturated fat, just as it has been for decades. 

If the FDA really wanted to inform the public about the risks in the food they eat, they would set maximum levels of salt, sugar and saturated fat per serving. As an example, if a can of baked beans had more than 300 mg of sodium per serving, that would require a warning label like those on cigarette packages.

Simply labeling something as "ultraprocessed" is meaningless. A piece of cheese is ultraprocessed because most people cannot make it in their home kitchen. Similarly, hamburger is ultraprocessed because most people cannot make it in their home kitchen. 

We need to stop the nonsense and focus upon the problem components: salt, sugar and saturated fats.

comments.body: Readers of the Times have likely read the Odyssey. Given the state of education in our nation, probably not so many. It makes me wonder if the writer/director read it. Nolan both wrote and directed it. It is the director’s vision. The vision seems myopic. For us who have read it, we will be watching it with a jaundiced eye. I’m also wondering if the casting of the female characters was some kind of statement. By the description of Circe, it seems like he heard about the pigs, heard the word witch, and thought of  Hansel and Gretel. Why avoid her entrancing sexuality? In a world increasingly unenthusiastic with DEI, he cast a Black woman. In 1200 B.C., there were nearly zero Africans in Sparta (although they were there 500 years later). Even though Homer’s description of Helen includes her arms being white, I can accept cross-cultural casting; we’ve been doing that for a while. My quibble is that she is not drop-dead beautiful enough to launch 1,000 ships. When it comes to the casting of Odysseus, he describes him as stocky. The criticism of Mr. Damon is that he doesn’t look Greek. I can get past that. There were fair-haired Greeks (Achilles is described as having reddish-blond hair). Homer describes him as stocky. Until he lost 20 pounds “for the role,” Mr. Damon fit that description. I understand that the director told him to “show up lean and strong, I’ I haven’t seen it yet. Perhaps IMAX will sweep me up.

CB built their business around locating stores near highway exits. Part of the charm was sitting in a rocker outside playing a game of jumbo-sized checkers while waiting for a table. These days, we’re all pressed for time, so the memory of waiting around makes us feel like Cracker Barrel is just too slow for a quick meal on the road.

comments.name: Stacy
comments.body:
I had Breast Cancer last year.  I also have a great gynaecologist. 

When we decided to finally remove a cyst I had growing on my ovary, she suggested, while having the laparoscopy surgery, to remove both fallopian tubes. She told me ovarian cancer almost always starts there. It wasn’t a difficult operation, recovery was easy, and peace of mind was even better. 

We had been discussing this for a couple of years, and I live on Ontario, Canada. The fact that so many specialists don’t know about this yet is shameful. I would actually suggest to all who plan on tubal ligation, to instead just have them removed. The ligation makes them useless and it would definitely save lives. Perhaps, to go a step further - anyone who is not having children or has reached menopause should think about removal, especially if they are having another procedure done or if there is a history or risk factors for cancer.  Ovaries still provide endocrine health without the tubes. It would cost $ for hospitals, but think of the people a new guideline like this, could save?

Of course, this life-saving information should be worldwide knowledge, and shamefully late in coming, for a couple tiny pieces of tissue that can kill, but it’s ‘women’s healthcare’, which is another topic entirely. 

If my gynaecologist in Ontario knew about this a few years ago, the info is out there. Shame on docs who don’t keep current. And kudos to NYT for spreading the word. 

Men, share this with women in your life, too!

comments.name: A geologist
comments.body:
I am compelled to respond when people argue countries do not manage forests & unprecedented fires better. It is bad information & misleading. It relies on finding simple villains.

In n. hemisphere large parts of Europe are drying out, desertification is creeping from Africa to the northern mediterranean.

Canada's vast sparsely populated boreal forests, over a million contiguous square miles from Nova Scotia to British Columbia/Yukon, are drying out.

The same goes for Russia's  larger boreal forests.

Southerly areas of permfrost are melting. The arctic is heating 3+ times faster than elsewhere. Agricultural growing zones are moving north.

All global trends are moving in a clear and persistent direction.

We are privileged to live within a range of ecological conditions and environmental constraints. These are being exceeded due to climate change. Our infrastructure was designed to function within min - max constraints, exceed criteria and it doesn’t function adaquately.

Many people essentially say there is nothing new under the sun (Ecleissiates). The thing is the tide goes in & out and "it gets hot, it gets cold" not by chance but established proven principles.

Popular bias and convention are problems for science. I get it, we don't like massive unprecedented change, we want stasis, but denying climate change with simple convienent views is blind and anti science. Views that will lead society to the dust heap of history as historians & geologist say.

comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
Many people are simply unaware of the scale of the threat which climate change poses to humanity.

The carbon cycle for the last 2 million years was doing 180-280ppm atmospheric CO2 over 10,000 years and we’ve done more change than that in 100 years.

The last time CO2 went from 180-280ppm global temperature increased by around 4 degrees C and sea level rose 130 meters. (graph of the last 400,000 years of global temperature, CO2 and sea level https://www.ces.fau.edu/nasa/images/impacts/slr-co2-temp-400000yrs.jpg )

One amplifying feedback alone out of dozens, loss of albedo or heat reflectivity from Arctic summer sea ice melt, over the last several decades has been equivalent to 25 percent of the climate forcing of anthropogenic CO2. And that will continue to increase as that ice largely disappears by mid century.

The Titanic sank because by the time the lookout called the warning the ship had too much momentum to turn. The Earth has a lot more momentum, e.g. we've already likely locked in at least 6 meters of sea level rise from the marine sectors of Greenland and West Antarctica’s ice sheets, and decade to decade warming in the near term is also virtually locked in.

That momentum is building and the higher we let global temperatures rise the greater the risk of them going really high as amplifying feedbacks strengthen.

The grief I felt has aged me - in my soul. But also on my face and in my body. I can SEE it. I'm in my 50s now, and I really can see how my face is changing into the older/old lady I will become. But I'm not touching my face right now. Not yet, at least. I've seen the beauty in growing old gracefully - I saw it on my father before he died. And I saw how youth can be taken in an instant. The utter, overwhelming tragedy of that. All life is fleeting. But precious. Aging is a part of this journey we're on, and I wish more women would just embrace their age. Welcome it even! And maybe when we look in the mirror, we don't see all that we've lost. But all that we are still *becoming*. That is truly the greatest gift of all.

Clearly this topic has struck a major artery, not a nerve. From 10 year olds stocking up on age defiers at Sephora, to Mar-a-Lago face, to deep plane facelifts, snail spem, to Clavicular (how I wish I didn't know who that is), and god knows what else, it seems like the entire population has gone down a rabbit hole of an attempt at eternal youthfullness. 

If I had put the gazillions (exagerating, but not by much), I spent from the age of 13 to 60, on serums, makeup, potions and lotions, dermatologists(!), and other promisers of fantastic "maintenence", etc.,etc., and instead put it in an interest bearing account, I'd be thinking about island beach real estate now.

The point, the soul, of this piece is not really about preserving youth and beauty. It is about the futile quest to stave of the inevitable and to remain visible while trying to do so. The author's mother is a totem in this journey, as are all of our parents. 

I hated my bulging knuckles for decades, then I realized they were exactly like my father's. Now I look at them in bittersweet happiness as a daily reminder of him whenever I use my hands.

I am one of three sisters whose dad used to say to my siblings “why aren’t you more like Leslie - she wears make-up and sews her own clothes”. Being daddy’s favorite taught me the power of beauty. Both my sisters and many of my friends have opted out of “fighting the good fight”. They seem perfectly happy. But one interesting note…when they attend a wedding and dress-up, I’ve noticed their personalities transform - much more lively and outgoing! I believe that the beauty veil gives them more confidence and this seems to make them happier. Just an observation. But I say ladies…pick your lane and don’t throw hate at the gals in a different lane.

Crazy as it may seem, I never was a fan of makeup. I am 24F now, and I have only worn a full face of makeup maybe 15 times in my life (which some of them being for cosplay lol). 

My mother used it religiously, with tightening face creams & wrinkle treatments. I remember her trying to teach me to do my makeup, and I was never brave enough to even put on eyeliner. In fact, I'm terrible at it.

Later on, when I experimented myself, not only did it feel like a waste of time, but I also found out that I'm allergic to most products that you put on your face. I also just hated how fake I felt.

From then on, I never wear makeup. I'm just me, no makeup, 100% of the time. I guess I'm looksmaxxing natural beauty. I'm not a showstopper by any means, but I don't get hung up on whether my appearance is important all the time. It doesn't matter.

It has saved me so much money, and you still get compliments... ones that are actually based on your true beauty. 

In the time of A.I., be something real.

As a winemaker in northern California, climate change and fires have become somewhat of a regularity for our industry. I cannot recall a vintage in almost the last decade that hasn't experienced some fire-related pressure. Our mantra has become "make the wine when you can", and when the vintage and yields are good, we do. 

These fires are coming amidst a very strong El Niño event; layer on top of it the continuing effects of climate change and the ingredients for fire conditions are prime.

Sadly this is normal for our industry now. Yet, our greatest existential challenge is finding a niche with the modern consumer. As most would-be wine drinkers change their relationship with alcohol, the wine industry is caught in yet another cycle of pivoting and adaptation. For many it is a gloomy time as wineries sell off, but I like to remind that wine has been adapting for centuries. From rock sheltered plantings in the Canary Islands, to the phylloxera crises, to wars and everything between, we are farmers and we find a way.

I was pleased to attend a 10am screening in IMAX. The theater was sold out, which I have only experienced at film festivals in recent years. While some Homer scholars have issues with Nolan's adaptation, I believe his screenplay does an exemplary job of rendering the ancient literature quite relevant for modern times.

The theme of honor is at the core of the tale Nolan tells. Odysseus regrets many of his decisions and actions. He has seen and done things that undercut an heroic portrait. He shares his story honestly and with contrition. He takes accountability as Penelope listens and Athena observes. The suffering of women is not shrugged off, nor is the violence of men. 

Honor. Accountability. Honesty. In a time when self-dealing, refusal to own mistakes, and dishonesty have become commonplace, Nolan's adaptation rings true and resonates. The film is well cast and much more than a captivating cinematic spectacle. Nolan has made the ancient modern in compelling fashion. Bravo.

There is no definitive evidence that Margaret Thatcher’s policies were a failure; until the 2008 financial crisis, they generated substantial wealth and lifted many into prosperity. However, the 2008 crash exposed the Achilles' heel of this economic model. Following the meltdown, the UK government faithfully replicated US rescue strategies, but while the US economy recovered, the UK faltered. This stagnation triggered severe intra-party and inter-party rifts within both Labour and the Conservatives. The resulting political bickering led to an unending debate on public services, paralyzing essential sectors from the NHS to education and trickling down to local administration.

Today, a significant number of City and Borough councils are either completely bankrupt or on the brink of financial collapse, a crisis mirrored across NHS trusts. For those passionately advocating for further nationalisation or devolution, the dire state of these local bodies serves as a grim harbinger of structural failure. Furthermore, evidence contradicts the claim that bringing railways back into public ownership benefits passengers, as £100 standard return tickets have now become the norm. Much like the bloated administrations seen in the NHS and local councils, it remains unclear how many unaccountable "fat cats" are currently thriving within these newly nationalised rail systems.

Conventional warfare leaves visible scars—explosions, fires, and destruction confined to a defined area. Biological warfare or  bioterrorism is a different menace: silent, borderless, and devastating. Unlike bombs, a biological attack may not be immediately apparent. Incubation periods, the nature of the agent, and the ability of physicians to diagnose swiftly all determine whether lives can be saved.
Bioterrorism lacks the “glamour” of conventional attacks, yet its impact can be catastrophic. Infectious agents can wipe out populations, cripple economies, and even target agriculture through agro‑terrorism. Tools like CRISPR have made genetic modification easier, raising fears of engineered pathogens designed to attack humans, animals, or crops. comments.name: Hyde Park
comments.body:
The statement cited near the end of the article that: “Chinese companies are not doing open source for the sake of open source itself; they are employing it at as a strategy, as a tool of the challenger”, is applicable to companies in all nations but it expresses only a half truth.  

In reality, open source programming has been more like a university spread around the world, offering free education to all.

This is behind the development of prominent open source software in many areas such as  word processing and multimedia players, including one in the new category AI, namely DeepSeek.  Wikipedia is of a similar type origin, an early competitor to expensive encyclopedia.  

Open source today is now of key value in the development of poor nations

The team of volunteer people, and now many paid people, around the world who check and help regulate open sources products, deserve thanks for their contributions. 

China, like India, the U.S., Japan, and South Korea, is special because its contributions to open source can accelerate the benefits, and heartaches, of AI to all nations, including itself.

comments.name: A
comments.body:
The genius of Bill Gates was not as a coder or engineer.

Instead, Gates made the MSDOS source code freely available so that any programmer in the world could build games and applications that could only run on MS DOS (i.e., not Apple DOS).

Thus, when Microsoft teamed up with IBM to bundle MS DOS with the IBM PC (and every PC clone thereafter), they beat out Apple in the apps market, and generated enormous revenue streams -- which live on today with Windows.

This is an analogy of what China's Moonshot is doing.

comments.name: Giuseppe Volta
comments.body:
Chinese open weight models are helping narrow one of the biggest AI divides: the gap between organizations that can afford frontier models and those that cannot. That is a positive development for innovation and competition.

At the same time, we should broaden the discussion beyond the usual concerns of privacy and security. A more subtle risk is cognitive influence. What if a model consistently nudges users toward polarization, individualism, or other value systems? The issue is not only what an AI knows, but the assumptions it quietly reinforces at scale.

For this reason, I found Pope Leo’s latest book particularly thought-provoking. Whether or not you share its perspective, it raises questions every technology leader should be asking. Highly recommended as a weekend read.

comments.name: C Christy
comments.body:
Kimi K3 is undeniably good tech held hostage by a government that can't decide if it wants Chinese AI to conquer the world or stay locked in a compound. "Open" is doing a lot of lying here: you can see the code, you just can't run it without a license and a chip allocation Beijing might yank anyway. That's not open source, that's a demo with a paywall and a leash.

Ask Kimi about June 4, 1989 and you'll get a wall, a redirect, or historical amnesia dressed up as a "sensitive topic." Ask about Taiwan and it'll recite the CCP's one-China script like it's reading from a Party memo, because it is. That's the tell: a model that can write code as well as GPT but can't tell you who runs Taiwan's government without genuflecting to Zhongnanhai isn't a technological triumph, it's state media with better math skills.

Can they out-compete Silicon Valley? On benchmarks, increasingly yes. On trust, no chance, because any system built to lie by design about its own government's atrocities will lie about whatever else serves the Party next. That's not a bug you patch, it's the whole architecture.

comments.name: Nits
comments.body:
The agitation has settled now, normalcy has returned, and parliamentary debates have begun. Both Left and Right political coalitions are competing for Gen Z.

CJP has handled the negotiations quite competently, and both the government and CJP have acted in good faith. The role of the Congress-led opposition appeared quite effective and constructive.

Gen Z is a smart lot, and neither Congress nor BJP will find it easy to persuade them. They cannot be swayed by religion or benefits, and are tech-savvy. Their thinking style, if their rap is any indication, appears to be different — it is a composite of multiple ideologies, a collage of sorts.

I don't think NY Times reporters really get a sense of what is happening in India. It is certainly not easy to figure out, and I make no claim to know it either. Maybe when we hear more from the real Gen Z folks out there — in essays, poems, and books — we will get a glimpse. 

Compared to what I have seen in West Bengal of 1970s and early 80s this is certainly a change for the better.

Meanwhile the students have shown remarkable moral character, volunteering to clear up the protest area.  I don’t know if it was the young girl saying with a smile, it is our responsibility to pick up all litter or if it was the young man telling other volunteers to go home since it was late at night and offered to take over, that made my eyes wet.  These young people have shown this spineless government what courage and responsibility looks like.  Shame on the Indian government to first callously let the students suffer and then punish them for asking which should be rightfully theirs anyway.  Remember, students shouldn’t have to protest for 36 days and go on a hunger strike for 23 days, to demand honesty in centralized testing.  It should be a given.

comments.name: Wim Roffel
comments.body:
This article is the latest crime of the "Let's fight till the last Ukrainian" tribe.

The Nuremberg and Tokio tribunals were a type of victor's justice. The Yugoslavia tribunal was that de facto too - although it also condemned a token few from the winning side. Saying that you want to apply that kind of "justice" in the Ukraine conflict is saying that you don't want the war to stop until a clear Ukrainian victory. As that time looks far away the implication is that you want the war to keep going on for a long time.

If you want international justice in Ukraine you should start at the beginning: the Maidan revolution of 2014. Under international law interference in the internal affairs of other countries is not allowed. Yet here we saw the complete Western Corps Diplomatique supporting an uprising.

Since then Ukraine hasn't been democratic. There were always the right-extremist militias to "corrrect" the government when it wasn't anti-Russian enough. Pushed by the US and its desire to absorb Ukraine into NATO this has led to the war. 

Real justice should include those Ukrainian militias. It should also include those Western leaders who signed the Minsk Agreements without the intention to implement them.

"People who are not professional historians sometimes assume that historical research is a once-and-for-all process that will eventually produce a single, final version of what happened in the past. But revisiting and often revising earlier interpretations is actually at the very core of what historians do. And that’s because the present is continually changing."

[National Council on Public History]

History is chaotic and particularly for the span of our lifetimes.

We are too close to readily understand the events.   Where in a Nation one is may expose different local standards for textbooks or even different attitudes in differing communities within a State or a Canadian Province.   How Alberta sees the Canadian Dominion likely is quite different from that way Quebec sees matters.    I expect that events in Paris or in Arles or in Champagne see different takes within France.

History is a mish-mosh of holdings and the Black community has its various takes even amongst its generation.

I live here.  Kumamoto Castle was already damaged in the devastating double-quake ten years ago, and now, just months after the 10 year celebration of the city's recovery, another almost identical disaster has happened.  Thousands of people are without access to water or power, in a summer where the afternoons are regularly hitting 95-98 degrees F, with humidity so intense you could choke, so suffocating that even sweat doesn't help you cool down.  A mall barely half an hour from my house collapsed, and then exploded in the aftermath, trapping dozens inside.  There was a preschool on the second floor of that mall.  We think the children made it out, but we don't know.  And the whole region is waiting with baited breath, because the last time this happened, in 2016, the first earthquake wasn't the worst.  Even when the aftershocks had calmed, the worst damage came a day later, with a second quake even stronger than the first.

We watched our city's symbol of resilience crumble today.  But the lessons Kumamoto and the greater island of Kyushu learned 10 years ago also mean that we have opened shelters and emergency provisioning stations faster than the last time.  My community responded within minutes that everyone was accounted for and uninjured.  We are shaken, but still standing.

And hoping desperately that the next week will be on stable ground.

I would expect markets to reverse course when hedge fund managers and institutional traders subsequently step in to readjust their positions. At least, that’s how I would read it.

Whether new technologies prove to be a giant bubble or a new industrial revolution, at a minimum, I suspect fierce competition will likely cause several overfunded AI companies and their supply chains to fail, resulting in financial turmoil. Perhaps governments should consider imposing excise taxes on these firms' revenues and on the capital they raise during an IPO to create contingency reserves that would help absorb potential financial shocks and mitigate any social and environmental harms.

A place where anyone (for a modest fee) could go and view art and be nourished by it is now a place for some people to view art as investment and be enriched financially by it. A place whose design was to keep out light to protect the art now looks like a place designed to keep out people to protect buyers and their deals. The museum restaurants were never cheap, museum restaurants never are, but they were part of something fantastic and, at their core, egalitarian, insofar as they were for the museum goers. Times change, don't they. I doubt the patrons of Marcel will be scared away now. Just as I doubt most readers would have gone there before being scared off. So maybe this review is a little useless. It is, however, a good encapsulation of what has happened in our city in general. Money has moved in big time. comments.body: For the first time in a long time, we know exactly where you stand on this one. You don't like it, you were disappointed, the food is not great, you say so clearly. It's refreshing. Much more useful than a review one has to parse to find a clear statement of evaluation. Which too often happens. The pictures as always make everything look divine. I find that disconcerting. But these days when so much restaurant fare is designed for the eye (well, the camera) and not the palate, the disjunction is inevitable when the food is bad. More surprising are your generalized digs at wealth. I'm neither wealthy nor a fan of wealth, but so many of the places you laud are hugely expensive and cater to wealth. Is it different here? Is it the Sotheby's connection? Are there no irreproachably tailored, oblivious men on computers eating lunch elsewhere? The digs seem mean. Nonetheless, Marcel is only satisfactory. We've been warned. It's not easy to come down hard on a place in an economy in which "satisfactory" could be damaging. I would say though that the reviews as a whole will seem more accurate, more thorough if "satisfactory" isn't only handed out to well-bankrolled places as it has been so far in the new regime, and if the main critics, not just the critics of the mini reviews, aren't shy to use it. comments.name: Erik Frederiksen
comments.body:
We are experiencing a very non linear increase of local and regional climate-related impacts surprising many scientists by how soon they are occurring: heat waves, droughts, wildfires, floods, stronger storms, etc.

This is in large part because ice melt, which reduces heat reflectivity, is causing the Arctic to warm around 4 times the rate of the whole planet and the decreased horizontal temperature gradient between the Arctic and the rest of the world has helped cause the northern polar jet stream to slow, and get stuck in wavy patterns.

These patterns bleed heat north and cold south, and cause weather systems to persist (like the heat wave that spread fire that incinerated Lytton, British Columbia a few years ago).

Also for every degree C rise in temperature the atmosphere can hold 7 percent more moisture, an exponential increase. Hence the “rain bombs” we’ve been seeing around the world.

As we get flooded by this from above the rate of sea level rise is accelerating and maximum storm strength is increasing.

There’s some adapting that we have to do to the changes already in the pipeline, but it wouldn’t take us long to make the changes too big to adapt to.

I attended this performance at Caramoor and loved every minute of it. This review does a nice job discussing the key individuals in the production, but I’m not sure how someone could review a performance like this without once mentioning the world-class performance by the orchestra. 

Period instruments often do not fare well in outdoor venues, but you wouldn’t know it from hearing this group — intonation was nearly flawless, strings had a warm and well-blended tone, woodwinds and brass soared in all the key moments, and the continuo group brought mature sensibility to its recit accompaniment. Much credit belongs to Whelan of course, but it’s baffling to see zero column space dedicated to the orchestra. 

This newspaper once called Philharmonia Baroque the leading period ensemble in the US. This performance at Caramoor certainly supports that notion.
